Nonlinear Instability in the 2D Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation

David M. Ambrose Address: Department of Mathematics, Drexel University, Philadelphia, PA 19104, USA Email address: dma68@drexel.edu , Anna L. Mazzucato Address: Department of Mathematics, Penn State University, University Park, PA 16802, USA Email address: alm24@psu.edu and Riccardo Montalto Address: Dipartimento di Matematica, Università degli Studi di Milano, Via Saldini 50, I-20133, Milano, Italy Email address: riccardo.montalto@unimi.it
Abstract.

In this paper we analyze the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (KSE), a model of flame-front propagation, on a two-dimensional square torus of arbitrary size 2​L2L with L>πL>\pi. In this case, the linearized equation at the origin admits a finite number of growing modes, which corresponds to the positive eigenvalues of the linear operator −Δ2−Δ-\Delta^{2}-\Delta. The problem of analyzing the long-time behavior of solutions of the 2D KSE in two spatial dimensions remains largely open; the only global existence results are for sufficiently small tori, or for sufficiently anisotropic and thin domains, due to the lack of good a priori estimates. The main purpose of this paper is to analyze the instability around growing modes at the nonlinear level. More precisely, we consider the maximal growing mode λ0\lambda_{0} and we show that there is a finite dimensional manifold of initial data of size ε{\varepsilon} arbitrarily small such that the corresponding solutions become of size O⁡(1)O(1) over a time-scale of order log⁡(ε−1)\log({\varepsilon}^{-1}). The proof is based on several ingredients such as a sharp quantitative construction of an approximate solution bifurcating from the maximal linearly growing mode, a fixed point argument with exponential weights to construct local in time solutions, and a continuation argument based on sharp energy estimates and para-differential calculus.

Key words and phrases:
Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations, growing modes, nonlinear instability, energy estimates, para-differential calculus

1. Introduction

In this work, we study the long-time dynamics of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (KSE for short) in two space dimensions under periodic boundary conditions. The KSE is a model for long-wave instability in dissipative systems and was derived from a coordinate-free model of interface dynamics for flame-front propagation in combustion [25, 26, 35]. Because the KSE models the dynamics of an interface, the most physical dimensions are 1 and 2.

The KSE is a non-linear, hyperdissipative evolution equation that has both a scalar form for a potential vv with a non-linearity in conservative form, and a vector form for its gradient with a Burgers-type nonlinearity. We employ the scalar form of the equation that can be written as:

∂tv+Δ2​v+Δ​v+Π⁡(|∇v|2)=0,x=(x1,x2)∈𝕋L2:=𝕋L×𝕋L,\partial_{t}v+\Delta^{2}v+\Delta v+\Pi(|\nabla v|^{2})=0,\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in{\mathbb{T}}^{2}_{L}:={\mathbb{T}}_{L}\times{\mathbb{T}}_{L},

where

𝕋L:=ℝ/(2​L​ℤ)≃[−L,L],{\mathbb{T}}_{L}:={\mathbb{R}}/(2L{\mathbb{Z}})\simeq[-L,L],

and Π​v:=v−12​L​∫𝕋L2v⁡(x)​𝑑x\Pi v:=v-\frac{1}{2L}\int_{{\mathbb{T}}^{2}_{L}}v(x)\,dx, v:ℝ2→ℝv:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{R}} is (2​L)(2L)-periodic with respect to x=(x1,x2).x=(x_{1},x_{2}). We note that we have chosen to use a square torus, rather than allowing two independent dimensions such as [0,L1]×[0,L2].[0,L_{1}]\times[0,L_{2}]. This is primarily for simplicity, so as not to over-complicate the proofs to be presented. An additional benefit, though, is that this choice also highlights how our results do not depend on any anisotropy in the problem. In particular, we are not relying on any thinness of the domain, and thus our results are genuinely two-dimensional.

We shall assume that

(1.1) L>π,L>\pi\,,

which gives rise to growing modes for the linearized operator. By rescaling the space variables xx, we can set the problem on the standard torus 𝕋2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}. Namely, we rescale

x↦ω​xwhereω:=πL,x\mapsto\omega x\quad\text{where}\quad\omega:=\frac{\pi}{L},

and we set

v⁡(x)=φ⁡(ω​x),v(x)={\varphi}(\omega x),

with

φ:ℝ2→ℝ2​π−periodic in both variables.{\varphi}:{\mathbb{R}}^{2}\to{\mathbb{R}}\quad 2\pi-\text{periodic in both variables.}

The equation for φ{\varphi} becomes

(1.2) ∂tφ+Δω2​φ+Δω​φ+ω2​Π​(|∇φ|2)=0,x=(x1,x2)∈𝕋2,\partial_{t}{\varphi}+\Delta^{2}_{\omega}{\varphi}+\Delta_{\omega}{\varphi}+\omega^{2}\Pi(|\nabla{\varphi}|^{2})=0,\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in{\mathbb{T}}^{2},

where

Δω:=ω2Δ,Δω2:=ω4Δ2=ω4(∂x12+∂x22)2.\Delta_{\omega}:=\omega^{2}\Delta,\quad\Delta_{\omega}^{2}:=\omega^{4}\Delta^{2}=\omega^{4}(\partial_{x_{1}}^{2}+\partial_{x_{2}}^{2})^{2}\,.

Written in terms of frequency, ω,\omega, the condition (1.1) becomes

(1.3) 0<ω<1.0<\omega<1\,.

We study the instability for the Cauchy problem

(1.4) {∂tφ=ℒω​φ−ω2​Π​(|∇φ|2),x=(x1,x2)∈𝕋2φ⁡(0,x)=φi​n​(x),\begin{cases}&\partial_{t}{\varphi}={\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}{\varphi}-\omega^{2}\Pi(|\nabla{\varphi}|^{2}),\quad x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in{\mathbb{T}}^{2}\\ &{\varphi}(0,x)={\varphi}_{in}(x),\end{cases}

where

ℒω:=−Δω2−Δω.{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}:=-\Delta_{\omega}^{2}-\Delta_{\omega}\,.

More precisely, we shall prove that for any 0<ε≪10<{\varepsilon}\ll 1 arbitrarily small, there exists a finite dimensional manifold of initial data of size O⁡(ε)O({\varepsilon}) in the Sobolev space HsH^{s}, for which there exists a unique solution φ{\varphi} up to time Tε≃log⁡(ε−1)T_{\varepsilon}\simeq\log({\varepsilon}^{-1}) such that ‖φ⁡(Tε)‖Hs=O⁡(1)\|{\varphi}(T_{\varepsilon})\|_{H^{s}}=O(1). For this result to hold, ss has to be taken large enough, specifically bigger than 44. We shall prove this result in the general case in which the linearized equation can have an arbitrary number of growing modes (positive eigenvalues of the linear operator ℒω{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}). The only hypothesis on the size of the torus, i.e. (1.1), guarantees that there is at least one strictly positive eigenvalue of ℒω{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}, as already mentioned.

The problem of studying the long-time dynamics of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (KSE) is far from being understood in dimension greater than 1. A main difficulty in proving global existence is the lack of a maximum principle for the KSE, due to the presence of the biharmonic operator. In dimension d=1d=1, it is possible to obtain an a priori estimate on the L2L^{2} norm of uu due to the special structure of the non-linearity, which can be written in divergence form. The L2L^{2} control allows to prove global existence by a continuation argument [39]. The one-dimensional global existence result of [39] allows exponential growth of solutions, because the linearized operator ∂t+Δ2+Δ\partial_{t}+\Delta^{2}+\Delta admits exponentially growing modes for large enough periods. It has then been demonstrated that this exponential growth does not actually occur, and solutions which start near the zero solution remain near the zero solution[16], [31]; this is sometimes described as stability of the zero solution in the one-dimensional KSE, but this is not stability in the usual sense in that it is not possible to control solutions to remain arbitrarily close to the zero solution.

For many well-studied equations such as the incompressible Navier-Stokes or Euler equations, the availability of an L2L^{2} estimate is independent of dimension. This situation is markedly different for the KSE. In fact, there is no known global estimate for any LpL^{p} norm in d>1d>1, and this is a primary reason why the issue of global existence of solutions to the KSE is still open.

There is an extensive literature concerning the KSE in dimension d=1d=1. While we do not survey the full literature in the one-dimensional case, we mention results concerning analyticity of solutions (see [8, 19] and references therein), optimal bounds on the growth of the L2L^{2} norm as a function of the period LL [7, 13, 14, 15, 32, 36, 37, 38] (see also [20]), and inertial manifolds [11, 21].

There are few results for the higher-dimensional KSE. Short-time existence and analyticity is known to hold in the full space with data in certain LpL^{p} spaces [6] (see also [20]). For d=2d=2, global existence holds for thin or sufficiently anisotropic domains [5, 24, 30, 34]. A first isotropic result was [2], in which Ambrose-Mazzucato studied the KSE on 𝕋2{\mathbb{T}}^{2} and proved short-time existence and analyticity with a bound on the analyticity radius for data in L2L^{2} and in the Wiener algebra. They established global existence of mild solutions for mean-free data sufficiently small in L2L^{2} and in the Wiener algebra, but only in the absence of growing modes, which happens in a two-dimensional torus [0,L1]×[0,L2][0,L_{1}]\times[0,L_{2}] when L1,L2<2​πL_{1},\;L_{2}<2\pi. Subsequently, Ambrose and Mazzucato extended this to global existence of small solutions when L1L_{1} and L2L_{2} are each slightly larger than 2​π,2\pi, so that there is a linearly growing mode present in both spatial directions [3]; this is the only isotropic global result for the higher-dimensional KSE which allows a linearly growing mode in each spatial direction. In [10], Feng-Mazzucato proved existence of mild solutions for sufficiently small data ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0) in L2L^{2} on an arbitrary interval of time [0,T][0,T] in the absence of growing modes. In [1], solutions of the KSE in arbitrary dimension are proved to exist when the initial data has low regularity, but the solutions are only global in the absence of linearly growing modes. We also mention a detailed numerical study of the two-dimensional KSE [22].

We only consider the classical form of KSE, and not any modified or generalized KSE, for which more results are known (see e.g. [12, 29]). One recent modified equation is the anisotropically reduced KSE [27], in which a maximum principle holds for one component of the gradient of the solution; another anisotropic modification of the KSE is studied in [41]. In [10], Feng and Mazzucato also considered the KSE with additional linear advection and prove that global existence can be achieved in the presence of growing modes and for arbitrary data, if the advecting field is relaxation enhancing with sufficiently small dissipation time. We also mention [9] where the advection term is given by a shear flow. Another work on equations similar in some ways to the KSE is [4], in which the question of global existence or singularity formation was studied for hyperviscous equations of Hamilton-Jacobi-type. We also mention the work [23] where a 1D KSE-type equation with a dispersive term is considered, showing that the dispersive term weakens the global bounds.

In the present paper, we study the KSE in the case of the two dimensional periodic box 𝕋L2:=(ℝ/(2​L​ℤ))2{\mathbb{T}}^{2}_{L}:=({\mathbb{R}}/(2L{\mathbb{Z}}))^{2} with L>πL>\pi, so that we allow the presence of an arbitrary large number of linearly growing modes. We rigorously prove instability, namely, we construct initial data of arbitrarily small size O⁡(ε)O({\varepsilon}) such that in finite time T≃log⁡(ε−1)T\simeq\log({\varepsilon}^{-1}) the corresponding solutions become of order O⁡(1)O(1) (in the HsH^{s} topology). Our approach is inspired by the technique developed in [17], in which the author proves some nonlinear instability results for the Euler and Prandtl equations (see also [18]).

We expand a function u∈L02​(𝕋2)u\in L^{2}_{0}({\mathbb{T}}^{2}) in Fourier series as

σ⁡(ℒω)={λω​(ξ)=−ω2​|ξ|2​(ω2​|ξ|2−1):ξ∈ℤ2∖{0}}.\sigma({\mathcal{L}}_{\omega})=\Big\{\lambda_{\omega}(\xi)=-\omega^{2}|\xi|^{2}(\omega^{2}|\xi|^{2}-1):\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\setminus\{0\}\Big\}\,.

2.1. Ideas of the proof

We consider initial data ε​φi​n{\varepsilon}{\varphi}_{in}, arbitrarily small, i.e. 0<ε≪10<{\varepsilon}\ll 1 where φi​n{\varphi}_{in} is an eigenfunction of ℒω{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}, normalized in HsH^{s}, associated to the biggest (positive) eigenvalue of ℒω{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}, i.e.

ℒω​φi​n=λ0​φi​n,‖φi​n‖Hs=1.{\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}{\varphi}_{in}=\lambda_{0}{\varphi}_{in},\quad\|{\varphi}_{in}\|_{H^{s}}=1\,.

{∂tφ1=ℒω​φ1φ1​(0,x)=ε​φi​n​(x)\begin{cases}\partial_{t}{\varphi}_{1}={\mathcal{L}}_{\omega}{\varphi}_{1}\\ {\varphi}_{1}(0,x)={\varepsilon}{\varphi}_{in}(x)\end{cases}

Appendix A Some tools from Para-differential calculus

In this appendix we shall collect some properties of para-differential operators. We also give all the proofs in the quantitative way needed in the rest of the paper. For an exhaustive theory of para-differential operators we refer to the monographs [28], [40].

Let ψ∈Cc∞​(ℝ)\psi\in C^{\infty}_{c}({\mathbb{R}}) be such that

(A.1) 0≤ψ≤1,\displaystyle 0\leq\psi\leq 1,
ψ(y)=1,∀y∈[−1/2,1/2],\displaystyle\psi(y)=1,\quad\forall y\in[-1/2,1/2]\,,
ψ(y)=0,∀y∈ℝ∖[−1,1].\displaystyle\psi(y)=0\,,\quad\forall y\in{\mathbb{R}}\setminus[-1,1]\,.

Given 0<δ<10<\delta<1, we let

(A.2) ψδ​(η,ξ):=ψ⁡(⟨η⟩δ​⟨ξ⟩),(η,ξ)∈ℝd×ℝd.\psi_{\delta}(\eta,\xi):=\psi\Big(\frac{\langle\eta\rangle}{\delta\langle\xi\rangle}\Big),\quad(\eta,\xi)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,.

We then define the paraproduct operator TaT_{a} for given a Sobolev functions a∈Hs0​(𝕋d)a\in H^{s_{0}}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), s0>d2s_{0}>\frac{d}{2}, as

(A.3) Ta​u​(x):=∑ξ∈ℤdσa​(x,ξ)​u^​(ξ)​ei​x⋅ξ,σa​(x,ξ):=∑η∈ℤdψδ​(η,ξ)​a^​(η)​ei​x⋅η.T_{a}u(x):=\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\sigma_{a}(x,\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)e^{{\rm i}x\cdot\xi}\,,\quad\sigma_{a}(x,\xi):=\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\psi_{\delta}(\eta,\xi)\widehat{a}(\eta)e^{{\rm i}x\cdot\eta}\,.

In the sequel, we do not emphasize the dependence of all constants on δ\delta since it has to be taken small enough but it is a fixed parameter. The following lemma holds.

which establishes the claimed estimate. ∎

Lemma A.4.

Let ρ>0\rho>0, s0>d/2s_{0}>d/2, a∈Hs0+ρ​(𝕋d)a\in H^{s_{0}+\rho}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), be real valued. Then for any s≥0s\geq 0, u∈Hs​(𝕋d)u\in H^{s}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), one has

∥(Ta∗−Ta)u∥Hs+ρ≲s,ρ∥a∥Hs0+ρ∥u∥Hs.\|(T_{a}^{*}-T_{a})u\|_{H^{s+\rho}}\lesssim_{s,\rho}\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+\rho}}\|u\|_{H^{s}}\,.
Proof.

A direct calculation shows that

Ta∗​u​(x)=∑η∈ℤd(∑ξ∈ℤdσ^a​(ξ−η,η)¯​u^​(ξ))​ei​η⋅x=∑η∈ℤd(∑ξ∈ℤdψδ​(ξ−η,η)​a^​(ξ−η)¯​u^​(ξ))​ei​η⋅xT_{a}^{*}u(x)=\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\overline{\widehat{\sigma}_{a}(\xi-\eta,\eta)}\widehat{u}(\xi)\Big)e^{{\rm i}\eta\cdot x}=\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\psi_{\delta}(\xi-\eta,\eta)\overline{\widehat{a}(\xi-\eta)}\widehat{u}(\xi)\Big)e^{{\rm i}\eta\cdot x}

Then, by the definition of ψδ\psi_{\delta} and using that aa is real valued (a^​(ξ−η)¯=a^​(η−ξ)\overline{\widehat{a}(\xi-\eta)}=\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)), we have that

Ta∗​u​(x)=∑η∈ℤd(∑ξ∈ℤdψδ​(η−ξ,η)​a^​(η−ξ)​u^​(ξ))​ei​η⋅x.T_{a}^{*}u(x)=\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\psi_{\delta}(\eta-\xi,\eta)\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)\Big)e^{{\rm i}\eta\cdot x}\,.

Thus ℛ:=Ta∗−Ta{\mathcal{R}}:=T_{a}^{*}-T_{a} is

ℛ​u​(x)=∑η∈ℤd∑ξ∈ℤdg⁡(η,ξ)​a^​(η−ξ)​u^​(ξ)​ei​x⋅η,{\mathcal{R}}u(x)=\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}g(\eta,\xi)\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)\widehat{u}(\xi)e^{{\rm i}x\cdot\eta}\,,

where

g⁡(η,ξ):=ψδ​(η−ξ,η)−ψδ​(η−ξ,ξ).g(\eta,\xi):=\psi_{\delta}(\eta-\xi,\eta)-\psi_{\delta}(\eta-\xi,\xi)\,.

and

|g⁡(η,ξ)|≤2∀(η,ξ)∈ℝd×ℝd.|g(\eta,\xi)|\leq 2\quad\forall(\eta,\xi)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\,.

We next study the support of gg. By the properties of the function ψδ\psi_{\delta}, one has that

supp⁡(g)⊆{(η,ξ)∈ℝd×ℝd:δ2​min​(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)≤⟨η−ξ⟩≤δ​max​(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)}.{\rm supp}(g)\subseteq\Big\{(\eta,\xi)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}:\frac{\delta}{2}{\rm min}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\leq\langle\eta-\xi\rangle\leq\delta{\rm max}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\Big\}\,.

Then if (η,ξ)∈supp⁡(g)(\eta,\xi)\in{\rm supp}(g), the following estimates hold for a positive constant C0>0C_{0}>0:

⟨η⟩≲⟨ξ⟩+⟨η−ξ⟩≲⟨ξ⟩+δ​max​(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)≤C0​(1+δ)​⟨ξ⟩+C0​δ​⟨η⟩,\displaystyle\langle\eta\rangle\lesssim\langle\xi\rangle+\langle\eta-\xi\rangle\lesssim\langle\xi\rangle+\delta{\rm max}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\leq C_{0}(1+\delta)\langle\xi\rangle+C_{0}\delta\langle\eta\rangle,
⟨ξ⟩≲⟨η⟩+⟨ξ−η⟩≲⟨η⟩+δ​max​(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)≤C0​(1+δ)​⟨η⟩+C0​δ​⟨ξ⟩.\displaystyle\langle\xi\rangle\lesssim\langle\eta\rangle+\langle\xi-\eta\rangle\lesssim\langle\eta\rangle+\delta{\rm max}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\leq C_{0}(1+\delta)\langle\eta\rangle+C_{0}\delta\langle\xi\rangle.

Hence, by choosing 0<δ≪10<\delta\ll 1 so small that 1−C0​δ>01-C_{0}\delta>0, we can conclude that

⟨ξ⟩≤K1​⟨η⟩,⟨η⟩≤K1​⟨ξ⟩,K1:=C0​(1+δ)1−C0​δ.\langle\xi\rangle\leq K_{1}\langle\eta\rangle,\quad\langle\eta\rangle\leq K_{1}\langle\xi\rangle,\quad K_{1}:=\frac{C_{0}(1+\delta)}{1-C_{0}\delta}.

The above inequality then also implies

⟨η⟩≲max⁡(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)≲min⁡(⟨η⟩,⟨ξ⟩)≲⟨η−ξ⟩.\langle\eta\rangle\lesssim{\rm max}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\lesssim{\rm min}(\langle\eta\rangle,\langle\xi\rangle)\lesssim\langle\eta-\xi\rangle\,.

Consequently,

(A.12) supp(g)⊆{(η,ξ)∈ℝd×ℝd:⟨η⟩≲⟨ξ⟩,⟨η⟩≲⟨η−ξ⟩}.{\rm supp}(g)\subseteq\Big\{(\eta,\xi)\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{R}}^{d}:\langle\eta\rangle\lesssim\langle\xi\rangle,\quad\langle\eta\rangle\lesssim\langle\eta-\xi\rangle\Big\}\,.

Now, by (A.12) for any (η,ξ)∈supp⁡(g)(\eta,\xi)\in{\rm supp}(g) it holds

⟨η⟩s+ρ=⟨η⟩s⟨η⟩ρ≲s,ρ⟨ξ⟩s⟨η−ξ⟩ρ.\langle\eta\rangle^{s+\rho}=\langle\eta\rangle^{s}\langle\eta\rangle^{\rho}\lesssim_{s,\rho}\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{\rho}.

Therefore, the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality, using that s0>d2s_{0}>\frac{d}{2} and ∑ξ⟨η−ξ⟩−2​s0=∑k⟨k⟩−2​s0=C⁡(s0)<+∞\sum_{\xi}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{-2s_{0}}=\sum_{k}\langle k\rangle^{-2s_{0}}=C(s_{0})<+\infty, gives

‖ℛ​u‖Hs+ρ2\displaystyle\|{\mathcal{R}}u\|_{H^{s+\rho}}^{2} ≤∑η∈ℤd(∑ξ∈ℤd⟨η⟩s+ρ​|g⁡(η,ξ)​‖a^​(η−ξ)‖​u^​(ξ)|)2\displaystyle\leq\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\langle\eta\rangle^{s+\rho}|g(\eta,\xi)||\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)||\widehat{u}(\xi)|\Big)^{2}
≲∑η∈ℤds,ρ⁡(∑ξ∈ℤd⟨η−ξ⟩ρ+s0​|g⁡(η,ξ)|​|a^​(η−ξ)|​⟨ξ⟩s​|u^​(ξ)|​1⟨η−ξ⟩s0)2\displaystyle\lesssim_{s,\rho}\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\Big(\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{\rho+s_{0}}|g(\eta,\xi)||\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)|\langle\xi\rangle^{s}|\widehat{u}(\xi)|\dfrac{1}{\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{s_{0}}}\Big)^{2}
≲∑ξ∈ℤds,ρ⁡⟨ξ⟩2​s|u^​(ξ)|∑η∈ℤd2⁡⟨η−ξ⟩2​(s0+ρ)​|a^​(η−ξ)|2≲‖u‖Hs2​‖a‖Hs0+ρ2,\displaystyle\lesssim_{s,\rho}\sum_{\xi\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\langle\xi\rangle^{2s}|\widehat{u}(\xi)|^{2}\sum_{\eta\in{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}}\langle\eta-\xi\rangle^{2(s_{0}+\rho)}|\widehat{a}(\eta-\xi)|^{2}\lesssim\|u\|_{H^{s}}^{2}\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+\rho}}^{2}\,,

which implies the claimed bound. ∎

From the last lemma we can deduce the following result.

Lemma A.5.

Let k∈{1,…,d}k\in\{1,\ldots,d\}, s0>d/2s_{0}>d/2, a∈Hs0+1​(𝕋d)a\in H^{s_{0}+1}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), be real valued. Then for any s≥0s\geq 0, u∈Hs​(𝕋d)u\in H^{s}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}), one has

∥[Ta∂xk+(Ta∂xk)∗]u∥Hs≲s∥a∥Hs0+1∥u∥Hs.\Big\|\Big[T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}+(T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}})^{*}\Big]u\Big\|_{H^{s}}\lesssim_{s}\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+1}}\|u\|_{H^{s}}\,.
Proof.

We set ℛa:=Ta∗−Ta{\mathcal{R}}_{a}:=T_{a}^{*}-T_{a}. Then

(Ta∂xk)∗+Ta∂xk\displaystyle(T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}})^{*}+T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}} =−∂xkTa∗+Ta∂xk=−∂xkTa+Ta∂xk−∂xkℛa\displaystyle=-\partial_{x_{k}}T_{a}^{*}+T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}=-\partial_{x_{k}}T_{a}+T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}-\partial_{x_{k}}{\mathcal{R}}_{a}
=−Ta∂xk+Ta∂xk−T∂xka−∂xkℛa=−T∂xka−∂xkℛa.\displaystyle=-T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}+T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}-T_{\partial_{x_{k}}a}-\partial_{x_{k}}{\mathcal{R}}_{a}=-T_{\partial_{x_{k}}a}-\partial_{x_{k}}{\mathcal{R}}_{a}\,.

By Lemma A.1, since a∈Hs0+1a\in H^{s_{0}+1}, s0>d2s_{0}>\frac{d}{2}, one has that for any s≥0s\geq 0,

∥T∂xka∥ℬ⁡(Hs)≲s∥∂xka∥Hs0≲s∥a∥Hs0+1.\|T_{\partial_{x_{k}}a}\|_{{\mathcal{B}}(H^{s})}\lesssim_{s}\|\partial_{x_{k}}a\|_{H^{s_{0}}}\lesssim_{s}\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+1}}\,.

Moreover, applying Lemma A.4 with ρ=1\rho=1 gives for any s≥0s\geq 0, u∈Hs​(𝕋d)u\in H^{s}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}),

‖∂xkℛa​u‖Hs\displaystyle\|\partial_{x_{k}}{\mathcal{R}}_{a}u\|_{H^{s}} ≤‖ℛa​u‖Hs+1≲‖a‖Hs0+1​‖u‖Hs,\displaystyle\leq\|{\mathcal{R}}_{a}u\|_{H^{s+1}}\lesssim\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+1}}\|u\|_{H^{s}}\,,

which concludes the proof. ∎

Lemma A.6.

Let 𝒮M{\mathcal{S}}_{M} be the mollifier defined in (5.16) and let s0>d2s_{0}>\frac{d}{2}, a∈Hs0+1​(𝕋d)a\in H^{s_{0}+1}({\mathbb{T}}^{d}). Then for any s≥0s\geq 0, one has that ∥[𝒮M,Ta∂xk]∥ℬ⁡(Hs)≲s∥a∥Hs0+1\|[{\mathcal{S}}_{M},T_{a}\partial_{x_{k}}]\|_{{\mathcal{B}}(H^{s})}\lesssim_{s}\|a\|_{H^{s_{0}+1}}.
